triage.reason: Common pediatric complaint of vomiting and feeding difficulty with a diagnosis reachable by history and exam, plus red flags to distinguish.

demographics: Physiologic reflux is nearly universal in healthy infants and usually resolves by 12–18 months
GERD is more often recognized in older children and adolescents, who report heartburn
More common in children with obesity
More common in children with neurologic impairment such as cerebral palsy

risk_factors.text: Infancy (immature lower esophageal sphincter and liquid diet)
Neurologic impairment such as cerebral palsy
Previous surgery on the esophagus or upper abdomen

comorbidities: Cerebral palsy and other neurologic conditions
family_history: Family history of GERD or reflux
social_history: Exposure to secondhand smoke in the home

chief_complaints.text: My chest burns after I eat

hpi.onset: Gradual; in infants spitting up begins in the first weeks to months of life, in older children symptoms build over weeks to months
hpi.duration: Recurrent episodes over weeks to months; infants often have daily symptoms for months
hpi.progression: Often improves with age in infants; in older children symptoms persist or worsen if untreated, and may become more frequent than twice a week
hpi.location: Chest and upper abdomen, sometimes rising into the throat
hpi.radiation: May rise from the stomach up into the chest and throat
hpi.quality: Burning or sour feeling; infants show arching and discomfort rather than describing pain
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; worse after large or fatty meals and when lying down
hpi.timing: After meals, especially within 30–60 minutes, and when lying flat or bending over
aggravating: Lying down or bending over soon after eating
relieving: Sitting up or sleeping with the head of the bed raised

associated_symptoms.text: Spitting up or vomiting after feeds
Cough or hoarseness, especially at night
Irritability or crying after feeds in infants

pertinent_negatives: Vomiting that started suddenly and is worsening
Blood in stool or black stools
Severe abdominal pain or a rigid abdomen
Symptoms that began only with a new medication

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot describe heartburn; they present with frequent spitting up, arching of the back, irritability after feeds, and feeding refusal. Most physiologic reflux resolves by 12–18 months.
Young children may localize discomfort to the upper abdomen rather than the chest and may have recurrent vomiting or poor appetite instead of classic heartburn.
Increased abdominal pressure worsens reflux; symptoms are more frequent and more likely to persist, and weight loss is a key part of management.

general.mild: Well-appearing, thriving, playful; comfortable between episodes
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable or irritable after feeds; otherwise alert and interactive
general.severe: Fussy or irritable, feeding poorly, may be underweight for age
general.critical: Ill-appearing, lethargic or inconsolable, signs of dehydration or respiratory distress

findings.maneuver: Plot weight, length/height and head circumference on a growth chart and compare with prior measurements
findings.finding: Growth following a normal curve, no weight loss or faltering

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants and check for organomegaly or masses
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without mass or organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant for a firm, olive-shaped mass
Inspect the abdomen for visible gastric waves or distension
findings.finding: No visible peristaltic waves or marked distension
No tonsillar exudate, drooling or obstruction; may show dental enamel erosion with chronic acid exposure

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields and assess work of breathing
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds, no wheeze, stridor or increased work of breathing

findings.maneuver: Assess tone, posture and developmental milestones
findings.finding: Age-appropriate tone and development without focal deficits

findings.maneuver: Assess mucous membranes, skin turgor, tears and capillary refill
findings.finding: Moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor and capillary refill, no dehydration

labs.caveat: Low ferritin suggests chronic occult blood loss from erosive esophagitis; check only if anemia or GI bleeding is suspected.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected anatomic cause such as malrotation, hiatal hernia, or stricture; not needed for typical reflux

findings.text: Free gastroesophageal reflux of contrast into the distal esophagus
Normal position of the duodenojejunal junction (no malrotation)
Hiatal hernia with part of the stomach above the diaphragm

imaging.preferred_when: Red flags, failure of acid suppression, or suspected esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis

findings.text: Erythema, erosions, or linear streaks in the distal esophagus (reflux esophagitis)
Mucosal eosinophils on biopsy suggesting eosinophilic esophagitis

imaging.preferred_when: Symptoms persist despite treatment or the diagnosis is unclear; correlates symptoms with acid exposure

findings.text: Increased acid exposure time with episodes correlating to symptoms
Non-acid or weakly acidic reflux episodes on impedance

imaging.preferred_when: Vomiting with concern for pyloric stenosis, obstruction, or other structural cause

findings.text: Thickened pyloric muscle suggesting pyloric stenosis (in infants)

initial.why: Screens for anemia from chronic esophagitis or another cause of vomiting
initial.only_if: red flags such as poor weight gain, hematemesis, or pallor

initial.why: Evaluates for anatomic causes such as malrotation, hiatal hernia, or stricture
initial.only_if: vomiting is bilious, projectile, or atypical, or an anatomic cause is suspected

confirmatory.why: Directly visualizes and biopsies the esophagus when reflux esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis is suspected or symptoms fail treatment
confirmatory.only_if: Directly visualizes and biopsies the esophagus when reflux esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis is suspected or symptoms fail treatment

confirmatory.why: Confirms pathologic acid reflux and correlates episodes with symptoms when the diagnosis is uncertain
confirmatory.only_if: Confirms pathologic acid reflux and correlates episodes with symptoms when the diagnosis is uncertain

supporting.why: Low ferritin supports iron deficiency from chronic esophagitis
Helps exclude pyloric stenosis or obstruction when vomiting is prominent
supporting.only_if: infant with forceful or projectile vomiting

not_indicated.why: Nonspecific and rarely changes management in uncomplicated reflux
Not needed unless dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from persistent vomiting is suspected
No role unless pancreatitis or epigastric pain is a concern
Not relevant in the pediatric population
Not routine for typical reflux without red flags or treatment failure
Not routine; reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or persistent symptoms

decision_points: Typical reflux in a thriving child is diagnosed clinically; testing is reserved for red flags or failure of lifestyle and acid-suppression therapy
Bilious or projectile vomiting, GI bleeding, poor weight gain, or neurologic symptoms warrant prompt evaluation for anatomic or other causes
Endoscopy is the test of choice when esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis is suspected

differential.name: Pyloric stenosis
differential.why_considered: Infant with frequent vomiting after feeds, which can be mistaken for reflux
differential.trigger: Forceful or projectile non-bilious vomiting in an infant around 3–6 weeks of age, especially with a hungry infant who feeds again after vomiting

history: Vomiting becomes forceful and projectile, often after every feed
Infant remains hungry and wants to feed again right after vomiting
Onset typically 3–6 weeks of age, not present from birth
Progressive worsening rather than the waxing and waning of reflux
exam: Palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
Visible gastric peristaltic waves across the upper abdomen
Signs of dehydration and weight loss
labs: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with low chloride
Elevated bicarbonate on basic metabolic panel
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound showing thickened and elongated pyloric muscle
Upper GI series with a string sign or double-track sign if ultrasound is equivocal

differential.name: Eosinophilic esophagitis
differential.why_considered: Older child with reflux-like symptoms, trouble swallowing, or food impaction that does not respond to acid suppression
differential.trigger: Dysphagia, food impaction, or reflux symptoms that persist despite an adequate trial of acid-reducing medicine

history: Trouble swallowing solid foods or episodes of food getting stuck
Personal or family history of asthma, eczema, or food allergy
Symptoms do not improve with acid suppression
exam: May show signs of atopic disease such as eczema or allergic rhinitis
labs: Allergy testing may identify food triggers
imaging: Endoscopy shows esophageal rings, furrows, white plaques, or a narrowed caliber
Esophageal biopsy with 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field

differential.name: Cow's milk protein allergy
differential.why_considered: Infant with spitting up, irritability, and feeding difficulty that looks like reflux

history: Symptoms begin with introduction of cow's milk formula or in a breastfed infant whose mother consumes dairy
Blood or mucus in the stool
Eczema or other atopic features
imaging: Endoscopy with biopsy showing eosinophils in the esophagus, stomach, or colon
Symptoms resolve after eliminating cow's milk protein

differential.name: Gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Vomiting and abdominal discomfort in a child

history: Acute onset over hours to a day rather than weeks to months
Diarrhea, fever, and sick contacts
Vomiting precedes or accompanies diarrhea
exam: Diffuse mild abdominal tenderness without localization

differential.name: Peptic ulcer disease
differential.why_considered: Epigastric pain and nausea in an older child or adolescent

history: Epigastric pain that may wake the child at night
Pain relieved or worsened by eating
Use of NSAIDs or history of H. pylori infection
imaging: Endoscopy showing an ulcer in the stomach or duodenum

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Chronic cough, especially at night, which can be attributed to reflux

history: Wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath
Symptoms triggered by exercise, cold air, or allergens
Personal or family history of atopy
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or hyperinflated

differential.name: Tracheoesophageal fistula or esophageal atresia
differential.why_considered: Feeding difficulties and coughing or choking with feeds in a newborn
differential.trigger: Coughing, choking, or cyanosis with the first feeds in a newborn, or inability to pass a nasogastric tube

history: Symptoms present from the first feed
Coughing, choking, or cyanosis during feeding
Polyhydramnios during pregnancy
exam: Inability to pass a nasogastric tube
Abdominal distension if a distal fistula is present
imaging: Chest and abdominal x-ray showing a coiled nasogastric tube or air in the stomach

severity.mild: Occasional spitting up or mild heartburn fewer than twice a week; child is thriving, feeding well, and growing normally; no red flags.
severity.moderate: Symptoms two or more times a week with discomfort, feeding refusal, or night-time cough; growth may be slightly affected but the child is not dehydrated or ill-appearing.
severity.severe: Frequent symptoms with poor weight gain, esophagitis, feeding aversion, or respiratory symptoms; may require endoscopy and escalation of therapy.
severity.critical: Not typical of reflux itself; consider a different diagnosis such as pyloric stenosis, obstruction, or sepsis if the child is ill-appearing, dehydrated, or has bilious or bloody vomiting.

red_flags.meaning: Suggests intestinal obstruction, malrotation with volvulus, or GI bleeding; needs urgent evaluation
Suggests pyloric stenosis or increased intracranial pressure

red_flags.finding: Poor weight gain or weight loss
red_flags.meaning: Suggests inadequate intake, malabsorption, or a more serious underlying condition
Suggests esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis

red_flags.finding: Respiratory distress, choking, or cyanosis with feeds
red_flags.meaning: Suggests aspiration, tracheoesophageal fistula, or airway compromise
Suggests infection, dehydration, or another systemic illness

red_flags.finding: Onset of symptoms after starting a new medication
red_flags.meaning: Suggests medication-induced reflux or another adverse effect

complications.name: Reflux esophagitis
clues: Heartburn that persists despite acid suppression

complications.name: Barrett's esophagus
clues: Endoscopy with intestinal metaplasia on biopsy

special_populations.differences: Physiologic reflux is nearly universal and usually resolves by 12–18 months; infants present with spitting up, arching, irritability after feeds, and feeding refusal rather than heartburn. Red flags such as projectile or bilious vomiting should prompt evaluation for pyloric stenosis or obstruction.
Young children may localize discomfort to the upper abdomen rather than the chest and may have recurrent vomiting or poor appetite instead of classic heartburn.
Increased abdominal pressure worsens reflux; symptoms are more frequent and more likely to persist, and weight management is an important part of care.

key_questions.question: What does your child do after feeding — do they spit up, arch their back, or seem uncomfortable?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent spitting up or post-feed arching and irritability in an infant; heartburn or sour taste in an older child

key_questions.question: How often do the symptoms happen, and how long have they been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms two or more times a week over weeks to months suggests GERD rather than occasional physiologic reflux

key_questions.question: When do the symptoms happen — after meals, when lying down, or at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse within 30–60 minutes after eating and when lying flat, which supports reflux

key_questions.question: Is the vomiting forceful or projectile, and what color is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Projectile or green (bilious) vomit suggests pyloric stenosis or obstruction, not simple reflux

key_questions.question: Is there any blood in the vomit or black or bloody stools?
key_questions.looking_for: GI bleeding suggests erosive esophagitis or another cause and needs prompt evaluation

key_questions.question: How is your child growing — have they been gaining weight normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor weight gain or weight loss suggests a more serious condition or inadequate intake

key_questions.question: Does your child have trouble swallowing or pain when swallowing?
key_questions.looking_for: Dysphagia or odynophagia suggests esophagitis, stricture, or eosinophilic esophagitis

key_questions.question: Does your child have a chronic cough, hoarseness, or breathing problems, especially at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal cough or hoarseness suggests reflux reaching the airway or an alternative diagnosis such as asthma

key_questions.question: What and how much is your child eating, and are there trigger foods?
key_questions.looking_for: Large meals, high-fat or spicy foods, and lying down after eating worsen symptoms

key_questions.question: Does anyone smoke in the home, or is your child exposed to secondhand smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Secondhand smoke exposure is a modifiable risk factor for reflux

key_questions.question: Does your child have any other medical conditions, such as cerebral palsy, cystic fibrosis, or asthma?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic impairment, cystic fibrosis, or asthma increase the likelihood and severity of GERD

key_questions.question: Is your child taking any medicines, especially for asthma, allergies, depression, or pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications such as albuterol, prednisone, diphenhydramine, amitriptyline, or ibuprofen can worsen reflux

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have reflux or GERD?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of GERD supports the diagnosis

reasoning_points: Age-appropriate presentation: infants with frequent spitting up, arching, and irritability after feeds; older children and teens with heartburn or sour taste
Symptoms occur two or more times a week and are worse after meals and when lying down
Symptoms improve with lifestyle changes such as smaller meals, staying upright after eating, and elevating the head of the bed
Growth and hydration are preserved in uncomplicated reflux
Red flags are absent: no bilious or projectile vomiting, no GI bleeding, no poor weight gain, no dysphagia, no respiratory distress
Alternative diagnoses such as pyloric stenosis, eosinophilic esophagitis, cow's milk protein allergy, gastroenteritis, peptic ulcer disease, and asthma are considered and excluded
Testing is reserved for red flags or failure of lifestyle and acid-suppression therapy

easy: Infant with daily spitting up after feeds who is otherwise thriving and growing normally
Older child or teen with classic heartburn after large or fatty meals that improves with antacids
Symptoms clearly worse when lying down and better when sitting upright
No red flags on history or examination
medium: Infant with irritability and feeding refusal but normal growth
Older child with chronic nocturnal cough attributed to reflux rather than asthma
Symptoms that persist despite lifestyle changes and require a trial of acid suppression
Overweight child or adolescent with frequent symptoms
hard: Infant with forceful vomiting concerning for pyloric stenosis
Older child with dysphagia or food impaction suggesting eosinophilic esophagitis
Infant with blood or mucus in the stool suggesting cow's milk protein allergy
Child with neurologic impairment such as cerebral palsy and atypical feeding symptoms
Symptoms that do not improve with acid suppression, requiring endoscopy or pH monitoring
